messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Figures: People in uniform, Military Topics: Talks about military, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Carry Weapon: carry weapon, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo has been a dentist for forty-five years, a man whose life was built on precision, quiet confidence, and the steady calm he offered patients in his chair. Now, at seventy, that foundation has crumbled. Eighteen months ago, he attended a summer jazz festival in the city park, an annual tradition he had continued after his wife, Elena, passed away. He was standing near the food stalls, enjoying the music, when the soundscape shattered. It was not a firecracker, but a series of sharp, percussive cracks that tore through the trombones and laughter. In the chaotic seconds that followed, Mateo saw a man a few feet away stumble and fall. He remembers the bewildered look on the man’s face, the dark stain spreading across his shirt. Mateo’s own body reacted before his mind could; he dropped to the ground, scrambling behind a large rubbish bin, his cheek pressed into the sticky, damp grass. He lay there, heart hammering, until the screaming subsided and was replaced by sirens and shouted commands from men in heavy tactical uniforms.

The memory of that day does not exist for Mateo as a coherent story. When he tries to recall it, to explain what happened, the words fail him. It comes back not as a narrative, but as a barrage of sensory fragments that feel utterly real and present. He will be rinsing a patient’s mouth and suddenly smell the coppery scent of blood mixed with popcorn, feeling the damp chill of the grass on his skin. The experience is so immediate and overwhelming that a wave of sheer panic floods his chest, forcing him to stop, to grip the counter until the world solidifies around him again. He has come to believe he is fundamentally a coward. The thought that runs in a relentless loop is that he did nothing, that he hid while others were hurt. He blames himself for not trying to help the man who fell, a self-recrimination that has become the constant, punishing background noise of his life.

This sense of pervasive threat now dictates his every move. Loud, unexpected sounds are the worst; a car backfiring on the street outside his office or a dropped tray in the next room sends a bolt of adrenaline through him, and he is instantly on high alert, his body braced for impact. In his own practice, a place he once commanded with ease, he finds himself watching his patients with a deep suspicion he knows is irrational. As he leans over them, tools in hand, he is not just checking their teeth but scanning their posture, their hands, their eyes, searching for any sign of aggression. Before a new patient even sits down, he has already located every exit from the examination room and the waiting area, mapping his escape. This constant vigilance is exhausting. Last month, a patient who was in the Army Reserve began talking about his recent training exercises. Mateo felt his throat tighten and his hands begin to shake. He mumbled an excuse about needing to check something and fled to his private office, unable to bear the conversation.

To manage this unceasing feeling of danger, Mateo has rearranged his life. He stopped watching the evening news entirely after a report on a mass shooting left him breathless and shaking for an hour. He no longer goes to crowded public places. In the pocket of his coat, he now always carries a heavy, old-fashioned wrench from his garage—it is solid and comforting in his palm, a secret promise of defense. These changes have not gone unnoticed. His daughter, noticing his profound isolation and jumpiness during a recent visit, finally confronted him. His inability to explain himself, to put the horror into words without being completely overcome, was what scared her the most. It was her tearful plea that finally brought him to therapy. Mateo is here not because he believes he can be fixed, but because he promised her he would try. He is terrified that talking about the event will unleash it permanently, but a small part of him hopes he might one day be able to sit in a room without first planning his escape.
